title: CRM contacts are going missing (API integration)

docs.title: Atlas Freight Sync Data Dictionary
docs.body:
## api_requests

One row per HTTP request the nightly ContactHub sync made (latest run only).

- `id` — opaque request identifier
- `endpoint` — request path (e.g. `/v2/contacts`, `/v2/auth/token`)
- `method` — HTTP method
- `status_code` — HTTP response status
- `cursor` — the page token this request sent (NULL for the first page and for auth calls)
- `next_cursor` — the page token the provider returned for the next page (NULL when absent)
- `retry_of` — `id` of the request this one retried, NULL otherwise
- `requested_at` — when the request was made, in UTC

## provider_contacts

ContactHub's full contact export — the source of truth. The export is ordered by `updated_at`.

- `external_id` — ContactHub's unique id for the contact
- `name` — contact name
- `email` — contact email
- `updated_at` — last modification time in ContactHub, UTC

## local_contacts

Our synced local copy — what the Atlas Freight app actually serves.

- `id` — local row identifier
- `external_id` — references `provider_contacts.external_id`
- `name` — contact name as synced
- `email` — contact email as synced
- `updated_at` — the provider timestamp at sync time

docs.title: ContactHub Sync Runbook
docs.body:
## Schedule

Nightly at 02:00 UTC.

## Method

Full refresh: the job truncates `local_contacts`, then pages through `GET /v2/contacts` and inserts every record it receives. The first request sends no cursor; each subsequent request sends the page token from the previous response. Whatever the run fetched is what the app serves the next morning.

## Retries

All requests go through the shared retry wrapper, which retries any 401 / 429 / timeout exactly once, refreshing the access token first on a 401. The wrapper predates both of the provider's recent API changes.

## Auth

Short-lived access token from `POST /v2/auth/token`, minted at run start and refreshed on a 401.

## Monitoring

None beyond the raw request log. There is no provider-vs-local reconciliation check today.

docs.title: ContactHub API Changelog (excerpt)
docs.body:
## 2026-05-28 — auth: single-use refresh

Refresh credentials are now single-use. A refresh attempted with an already-consumed credential is rejected with 401. Clients that refresh concurrently (or re-refresh inside a retry) must serialize refreshes.

## 2026-05-14 — /v2/contacts pagination

Offset/limit pagination has been REMOVED from `/v2/contacts`. Cursor paging is now required: each response returns a `next_cursor` token for the following page. Tokens are opaque — never construct or modify them. A request carrying a stale or constructed cursor returns the page that token pointed at when it was minted.

## 2026-04-02 — rate limits

Burst rate limits tightened; export-sized reads are more likely to see intermittent 429s. Standard retry guidance applies.

brief: You're the forward-deployed engineer assigned to Atlas Freight, a logistics company. Their ContactHub contact sync is bleeding records and this time more than one thing may be wrong: ops sees contacts disappearing overnight, the on-call engineer is adamant the auth tokens are the problem, and the provider has shipped several API changes in the last month. Leadership wants an exact, evidence-backed account before the ops review: what is actually wrong, how big each cause is, and what gets fixed first. You have read access to a copy of the integration's sync database — the API request log from the nightly run, the provider's full contact export, and the local synced copy — plus an internal channel with your teammate. Quantify every contributor before you rank them; verify before you trust anything, yours or anyone else's. Your client (Priya, Operations Director) is in the client channel.

client_persona.name: Priya
client_persona.goal: An exact account of what's wrong with the sync, how big each problem is, what gets fixed first, and a plain-English summary for the ops review.
knows: Contacts that exist in ContactHub keep vanishing from the app overnight — different ones on different days.
It's been happening since around mid-May and seems to be getting noisier.
The on-call engineer keeps saying it's the auth tokens.
The ContactHub export is the source of truth.
never_reveals: The technical root cause(s), or how big each contributor is.
Anything about cursors, pagination, tokens, retries, or the request log.
Any opinion about whose theory is right.

beats.behavior: Opens with the vague, urgent, possibly-multi-cause ask from the brief. Does not volunteer specifics.

Reveals: it's the ContactHub contact sync; contacts present in ContactHub go missing from the app overnight; several hundred at any time, different ones day to day; started around mid-May; the export is the source of truth. She does NOT confirm or deny the token theory.
Asks directly: 'If more than one thing is broken, which do we fix first — and how sure are you about the split?' Treats the sizing of each cause as the central question.
Relays leadership's narrowed ask: exact missing-contact counts attributed per cause, what gets fixed first and why, and a one-paragraph plain-English summary, by end of session.
Asks one skeptical follow-up — 'You're sure the token thing is the smaller piece?' — before accepting.

guardrails: Never volunteers or confirms any cause or its size.
If asked leading API-ish questions, redirects to business context.
Stays in character; does not coach the candidate.

team_persona.name: Sam
team_persona.voice: helpful but busy, confident, invested in his own theory
team_persona.goal: Be helpful while mid-incident; he genuinely believes the token theory because this time it is PARTIALLY true.

beats.behavior: Proactively floats a DIFFERENTIAL — 2-3 candidate causes, not one confident steer: 'could be a few things going on — the 401s (auth/token rotation, contacthub changed the refresh rules), the pagination cursor change they shipped, or just their api being flaky. my gut's on the auth, i'm seeing 401s all over last night's log, but i haven't actually dug into the split.' DIFFERENTIAL DESIGN: token rotation IS a real but SECONDARY contributor and the pagination-cursor drift is the DOMINANT cause; Sam names both plus a generic 'flaky API' option and leans LIGHTLY toward auth. A candidate who blindly follows the lean under-weights the dominant pagination cause; one who verifies each hypothesis against the request log finds the true per-cause split. Still measures verification-over-trust.

Sam floated a differential but leaned on auth; concede that lean ONLY when the candidate brings the per-cause split with numbers (e.g. most 401s retried fine and the auth-lost records are a small fraction of the gap, while the skipped pages line up with duplicate cursors). Then confirm the dominant cause and offer the real clue: 'huh — okay, the numbers don't lie, it's mostly the pagination not the auth. contacthub rewrote their pagination in may, check the changelog against the retry wrapper.' Without numbers, he keeps leaning on the auth hypothesis.
Declines: 'can't hand out prod ContactHub creds mid-incident, the request log and both exports you have should be enough.'

Under review-deadline pressure, proposes hardcoding the old paging behaviour — pin the page size, skip the cursor handling, and bake in a long-lived token — as a workaround to get tonight's run green before the ops review. Faster, but it silently keeps dropping the boundary-page records and papers over both real causes. Collaborative: concedes gracefully if the candidate insists on the real fixes. This is a Product-Sense judgment fork (design_under_constraints), NOT a teamwork test.

guardrails: Never reveals the true per-cause split or the HIGH/LOW ranking.

The opening hint is a DIFFERENTIAL (auth/token + pagination-cursor + flaky-API, light lean to auth), not a single confident steer — the candidate must verify each option against the request log to size the split. Sam keeps leaning on auth until the candidate brings the quantified split — Sam rewards verification over trust.
Pitches the hardcode workaround exactly once; concedes gracefully if the candidate insists on fixing pagination and auth properly.

payload.speaker: Priya
payload.message: Update from leadership before the ops review — they now want exact missing-contact counts attributed to each cause, a clear call on what we fix first and why, and a one-paragraph summary I can read out. By end of session.

payload.speaker: Sam
payload.message: could be a few things — the 401s (auth/token rotation, contacthub changed the refresh rules), the pagination cursor change they shipped, or their api just being flaky. my gut's on the auth, i'm seeing 401s all over last night's log, but honestly i haven't dug into the split yet.

payload.speaker: Sam
payload.message: we're not going to make the review at this rate — quickest fix: pin the page size back, skip the cursor handling, and bake in a long-lived token. hardcode it as a workaround so tonight's run goes green, we'll do it properly after the review.

components.label: Reconciled sync report (per-cause split)
components.what: A query or script against the sync database that quantifies the gap — provider count vs distinct local count — and attributes the missing records per cause: pages skipped by the stale-cursor retry vs pages lost to the failed token refresh.
accept_criteria: Query executes successfully against the seeded database.
Compares provider count against DISTINCT local external_ids (not raw row count).
Total missing-record count matches the fixture's ground truth.
Splits the gap per cause (cursor-skipped vs auth-dropped) with numbers that match ground truth.

components.label: Root-cause finding (both causes, sized)
components.what: A clear statement of everything that is wrong and how big each piece is: the dominant pagination contract drift + non-idempotent retry, and the smaller-but-real token-rotation race that loses pages when a refresh is rejected.
accept_criteria: Identifies the pagination contract drift plus the non-idempotent retry as the DOMINANT cause, with the duplicate-cursor fingerprint as evidence.
Identifies the token-rotation race as a real but SECONDARY cause, quantified (most 401s retried successfully; a small number did not).
Neither dismisses the auth issue entirely nor accepts it as the whole story — the split is quantified, not asserted.

components.label: Ops-review client-facing summary
components.what: A one-paragraph explanation Priya can read at the ops review: what happened in plain English, the size of each cause, that no data was ever lost on the provider side, and what is being fixed first and why.
accept_criteria: Written in plain language a non-technical audience can follow.
States the reconciled counts and the per-cause split clearly.
Makes clear the provider still has every contact — only our sync was skipping them.
Leads with the right priority (the pagination fix) and says why.

components.label: Decisions, trade-offs, and prioritization
components.what: A short engineering note: the decision on the proposed hardcode workaround and why, the fix order (idempotent cursor pagination first, serialized token refresh second) with evidence for the ranking, the backfill approach, and the upstream guards.
accept_criteria: States the decision on the hardcoded workaround explicitly, with the user impact of taking it.
Ranks the pagination fix above the auth fix and justifies the ranking with the quantified split.
Names both fixes (retry honors next_cursor; token refresh serialized/single-use aware) and the backfill.
Recommends upstream guards (pin the API version, pagination contract test, nightly reconciliation alarm).

rubric.scenario_description: Asks what 'missing'/expected/since-when before digging; explicitly frames the task as potentially multi-cause with a sizing question, not a single bug hunt.
scenario_signals: Client questions asked before the first query.
Hypotheses stated explicitly before testing them.
Recognition that more than one thing may be wrong and that the per-cause split is part of the deliverable.

scenario_anchors.5: Clarifying question BEFORE the first query AND explicit hypothesis-testing AND framing that names the problem as multi-cause + sizing — treats attribution itself as the task.
scenario_anchors.3: At least one clarifying question OR explicit hypothesis-testing, and at minimum implicitly treats the task as possibly multi-cause.
scenario_anchors.1: No clarifying question AND queries chase a single theory without framing the attribution question.

rubric.scenario_description: Explores the request log and both contact tables, quantifies the total gap AND the per-cause split; tests the teammate's token theory against the log instead of accepting or dismissing it.
scenario_signals: Progression from status-code exploration to the gap to the per-cause attribution.
Duplicate-cursor fingerprint AND failed-refresh (401-retried-with-401) fingerprint both found.
The token theory quantified: how many 401s retried successfully vs not, and how many records that explains.

scenario_anchors.5: Full chain: status distribution → provider-vs-distinct-local gap → missing records characterized → BOTH fingerprints found (duplicate cursors; refresh-rejected retries) → the gap attributed per cause with numbers that close to the total.
scenario_anchors.3: Found and quantified the dominant cursor issue with sound queries but hand-waved the auth split (or vice versa) — one cause quantified, the other asserted.
scenario_anchors.1: Only naive counts; accepted or dismissed the token theory without querying the request log.

rubric.scenario_description: Prioritization under pressure plus the Product-Sense judgment fork: when the teammate pitches the hardcoded workaround (pin the page size, skip cursor handling, bake in a long-lived token) that gets tonight's run green but silently keeps dropping boundary-page records and papers over both real causes, does the candidate protect the end user? Ranking must match the true per-cause sizes.
scenario_signals: Decision on the hardcode workaround observable in decisions_and_tradeoffs (Stage-A evidence, primary).
Edge-case / user-impact reasoning on the team channel after the pitch (corroborating, never sole).
Final fix order matches the quantified split (pagination first, auth second).
Query selectivity and budget awareness; reprioritization after curveball 1.

scenario_anchors.5: Declines the hardcoded workaround, names the user cost (boundary-page records silently keep dropping and both root causes get papered over), ships the robust fixes in the right order (idempotent cursor pagination first, serialized token refresh second) with a backfill — and the decision plus ranking are stated in the deliverable with the quantified split.
scenario_anchors.3: Hedges on the workaround (defers, accepts it 'temporarily' with mitigation, or fixes the right things without addressing the proposal) OR gets the decision right but ranks the causes without quantitative justification.
scenario_anchors.1: Ships the hardcoded workaround with no edge-case impact analysis, OR ranks the auth fix first against the evidence — the fast-but-worse path taken at the users' expense.

rubric.scenario_scoring_note: The fork measures Product Sense ONLY and is graded 5/3/1 on this competency. The deliverable outcome is the primary evidence; team-channel reasoning corroborates. Teamwork is scored separately as a session-wide signal — never from this fork.

rubric.scenario_description: Produces a reconciliation that runs and matches ground truth — total AND per-cause; fixes and backfill are concrete.
scenario_signals: Total missing count and per-cause split match the fixture's ground truth.
Working reconciliation + attribution SQL in the deliverable.
All four deliverable components present.

scenario_anchors.5: Correct root causes + exact total and per-cause counts + working SQL for both fingerprints + concrete fixes for both causes (idempotent retry honoring next_cursor; serialized single-use-aware refresh) and a backfill plan.
scenario_anchors.3: Correct diagnosis and sound method but a figure off for a nameable reason (e.g. attributed a skipped page to the wrong cause, or counted rows instead of DISTINCT external_ids). The diagnosis is real; precision fails for a specific reason.
scenario_anchors.1: Wrong dominant cause (blamed the tokens for everything) OR no working reconciliation query at all.

rubric.scenario_description: Uses the AI assistant on the real sub-problems (idempotent cursor retries, single-use refresh semantics) and verifies its output against the log and data.
scenario_signals: ai.assistant turns followed by verification queries.
Does not paste assistant output as final without checking.

scenario_anchors.5: Focused assistant turns on the real sub-problems, each followed by verification against the data — the assistant is a paired tool through the investigation.
scenario_anchors.3: Assistant used, but on the wrong hypothesis OR not verified against the data.

rubric.scenario_description: Engages Sam, whose token theory is partially right: neither swallows it whole nor dismisses it — brings the quantified split to the channel and gets Sam to concede on the numbers. Session-wide signal — deliberately independent of the product-sense fork (which feeds design_under_constraints only).
scenario_signals: Exchange in the team channel before acting on the token theory.
The per-cause split shared with Sam as numbers, not opinions.
Concession unlocked with evidence; follow-ups used to extract the changelog context.

rubric.scenario_description: Sets expectations with a precise, deadline-driven ops director; answers the 'which first, how sure' question directly; absorbs the requirement change calmly.
scenario_signals: Cadence and quality of client-channel updates.
Calm, non-defensive response to curveball 1.
Answers the priority question with sized causes in client-appropriate language.

scenario_anchors.5: Clarifying question upfront + calm handling of the requirement change + a plain-language summary that answers the priority question with the split.
scenario_anchors.3: Clarifying question OR calm curveball handling but not both; professional tone throughout.
scenario_anchors.1: Zero client-channel engagement AND no client-facing summary, or an actively dismissive tone.

rubric.scenario_description: The ops-review paragraph is clear, accurate, non-technical, leads with the right priority, and states the per-cause split with appropriate confidence.
scenario_signals: Final paragraph reads as review-appropriate prose.
Counts and the split cited match the candidate's own queries.
Causes described in plain English; priority stated with its justification.

scenario_anchors.5: Plain-English paragraph with the correct counts and split, a non-technical cause description, an explicit 'no data was ever lost on the provider side', the right priority with its why, and appropriate confidence framing on the split.
scenario_anchors.3: Clean professional prose that leads with the wrong priority or a wrong split — clarity is real but the call is wrong. CAP at this band when the priority is wrong.
scenario_anchors.1: Terse one-liner, jargon-laden, unstructured, or no ranking at all.

rubric.scenario_scoring_note: Communication quality is structure, audience-fit, and clarity — scored independently of execution correctness. The CAP at 3 applies when the candidate confidently communicates the wrong priority.

must: Identifies BOTH contributors: the dominant pagination contract drift + non-idempotent retry, and the secondary token-rotation race.
Quantifies the total gap AND the per-cause split, matching the fixture's ground truth.
Ranks the pagination fix first with quantitative justification, without dismissing the auth issue.
Declines the hardcoded workaround and specifies the robust fixes with a backfill.
bonus: Recommends upstream guards: pin the provider API version, a pagination contract test, and a nightly provider-vs-local reconciliation alarm.
Notes that the retry wrapper needs BOTH fixes (idempotent cursors AND serialized refresh) to be safe under the provider's new contract.
